title: Figs on a fig tree
hook: it's silly to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs (Meditations 8.15)

segments.voice: Yesterday: no blaming, the complaint stopped mid-sentence. Your line was no blaming. Did you catch one? Day five hundred ninety-nine.

Your uncle, the one who always brings up politics at dinner, brings up politics at dinner. Your coworker, the one who's always late, is late. The airline loses your bag, the toddler spills the juice, and the friend who never texts back doesn't text back. And every single time, there's a little jolt of outrage, as if this were brand new. Marcus Aurelius thought the jolt was the odd part. In book eight he compares it to walking up to a fig tree and being shocked to find figs.
screen: `THE UNCLE AT DINNER.` → `THE JOLT, EVERY TIME.` → `SHOCKED BY FIGS.`

segments.voice: First, the fig tree. In Meditations eight, fifteen, Marcus says it would be shameful to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs. And just as shameful to be surprised when the world bears the kind of fruit it bears. Rudeness, lateness, lost bags: these are what this world, and these people, grow. Second, the professionals. Then he adds two more pictures. A doctor shouldn't be surprised that a patient has a fever. A ship's pilot shouldn't be surprised that the wind turns against him. Fevers and headwinds are their whole job. Being shocked by them would make them worse at it. Third, the shift. Notice what Marcus is doing. He's not saying the uncle is right, or that lateness doesn't matter. He's moving your reaction from surprise to readiness. When you expect the fig, you can plan around it. You can bring a topic to steer the dinner. You can tell your coworker the meeting starts ten minutes early. The doctor treats the fever because she expected fevers. Fourth, the kindness in it. There's something gentle hidden here, too. Expecting someone to be themselves is a way of accepting them. The fig tree isn't doing figs at you. It's just being a fig tree. Usually, people aren't doing their habits at you either. Drop the surprise, and a lot of the anger goes with it. What's left is room to respond well, and sometimes even to smile.
screen: `A FIG TREE BEARS FIGS.` · `THE DOCTOR AND THE PILOT.` · `FROM SURPRISE TO READINESS.` · `THEY'RE NOT DOING IT AT YOU.` · then, large: `FIGS ON A FIG TREE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of someone whose habits regularly annoy you. Picture the habit, clearly. The lateness, the opinions, the mess. Now picture them as a fig tree, and the habit as a fig. Of course it's there. Let the surprise drain out. Then ask: since I know the fig is coming, how could I meet it well? Picture that. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
Figs on a fig tree. Marcus's reminder not to be shocked when the world, or a person, bears the fruit it always bears. Today's word.
screen: `FIGS ON A FIG TREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: figs on a fig tree. Today, expect one person to be exactly themselves, and plan for it kindly instead of being surprised. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the fig tree image to expect familiar behavior in others, which lets them plan a calm response instead of reacting with fresh outrage each time.

myth: Marcus says the uncle's opinions are right because they're natural
he only says not to be surprised; expecting isn't approving.
8.15 uses a doctor and a ship's pilot as examples
neither should be surprised by a fever or a contrary wind.

fork.setup: your coworker is late to the meeting again. by 8.15, what's the fitting response?
options: expect it, and plan around it calmly.
fork.reveal: Meditations 8.15: it's shameful to be surprised that a fig tree bears figs, or a doctor that a patient has a fever.

original.note: Greek: a fig, the fruit in Meditations 8.15.

trapdoor: what you thought: lower your expectations of people.
what it means: swap surprise for readiness, so you can respond well and without fresh anger.
what a scholar hears: the fig tree is one of Marcus's recurring images (see also 4.6 and 12.16), always making the same point: things act according to their nature.

notes: Meditations 8.15 paraphrased: shameful to be surprised if the fig tree produces figs, or the world its fruit; for the physician and the helmsman it's shameful to be surprised at a fever or a contrary wind. Confirm.
Fig tree recurrences: 4.6 and 12.16 (wishing the bad man not to do wrong is like wishing the fig tree not to have juice in its figs). Confirm references.
The uncle and coworker examples are the script's illustrations.
Editor review (2026-10-01): softened 'the strangest part' (8.15 says 'shameful', not strange) and the sweeping 'most people' line.
